newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Yeltsin to visit Ukraine, strike friendship.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to visit Ukraine, strike friendship.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was to start his first state visit to Ukraine on Friday, described by the Kremlin as his main foreign policy step this year and by observers as the end of a "cold war" between Moscow and Kiev.
Yeltsin, who has postponed visiting Kiev at least six times in the last six years, will sign with Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma a long-awaited friendship treaty between the two Slav states.
"(It is) the most difficult visit and the most important foreign policy act by the Russian President in 1997," Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.

Moscow and Kiev, which played crucial roles in ending the Soviet Union in late 1991, have since found themselves caught up in a web of mutual recriminations over the heritage of the defunct communist empire.
Rows over the disputed Black Sea Fleet, Ukraine's energy debt and the fate of Soviet nuclear missiles have combined with other problems to sour bilateral relations.

"Yeltsin's visit to Kiev and massive talks held ahead of it herald a broad political agreement which is expected to take away the huge strains of the undeclared cold war between two former 'sister-republics'," Ukraine's Moloda daily wrote.

Kuchma and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin announced after three hours of talks in Kiev on Wednesday that they had managed to sort out all bilateral problems, including the shareout of the Black Sea fleet.

Under the deal signed by Chernomyrdin and Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, Russia won a 20-year lease of the naval base of Sevastopol in Urkaine's Crimean peninsula to keep its lion's share of the rusting Soviet-era force.
Lazarenko and Chernomyrdin also announced that they had managed to solve most issues in the struggling bilateral trade.

"The draw was in Kiev's favour," Moloda wrote, referring to the fleet deal in which the Kremlin clearly ignored demands by influential Russian nationalists to challenge Ukraine's right to own Sevastopol.
The decision stirred emotions among nationalists in Kiev who according to the respected Den daily were planning to greet Yeltsin "like hooligans" with protests against his visit.
Den suggested that Moscow's new commitment to seal a friendship treaty with Kiev and solve all outstanding problems was part of the Kremlin's wider political game with NATO.
Yeltsin signed a deal which gave Moscow some say in the Western alliance in exchange for an unspoken assent to NATO's plans to grant membership to some Eastern European countries.

But bowing reluctantly to the inevitable admission to NATO of Moscow's Cold War allies in the Warsaw pact, the Kremlin underlined that it would not tolerate granting membership to former Soviet republics.
Three Baltic States of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania are seeking full membership of NATO and Moscow had feared that Ukraine might follow suit.

"Delaying further the settlements with Ukraine, Russia would risk facing highly undesirable geopolitical results," Den wrote. "Annoyed and cornered Ukraine could rush to seek the protection of the West."

On Thursday, a day after solving its problems with Russia, Ukraine tacitly accepted that it would not seek NATO membership by initialling a separate security pact with the Western alliance in the Portugese town of Sintra.
The deal, like Russia's although narrower in scope, is not seen by Moscow as a threat to its interests.
"Keeping Ukraine away from drifting towards NATO is a far more important task for Russia now than trying to get the whole of Sevastopol for the Russian navy forever," Den added.
The Kremlin appeared to agree with such a linkage. "The closer the ties between Russia and Ukraine, the fewer the headaches in its (Russia's) relations with NATO," Yastrzhembsy said.
